newsitem.title: USA: White House panel recommends air safety measures.
newsitem.headline: White House panel recommends air safety measures.

text.p: Reacting to increased public concern about air safety, a White House commission on Wednesday proposed measures to reduce the number of fatal air accidents by 80 percent over the next 10 years.

Vice President Al Gore, speaking at the commission's final meeting, said its key goals were "to dramatically reduce the rate of fatal accidents," to speed up the modernisation of the U.S. air traffic control system and to intensify the fight against terrorism.

Gore said the National Aeronautics and Space Administration would announce later on Wednesday a programme of air safety research that would cost $500 million over five years. This was "in response to our goal to reduce fatal accidents by 80 percent over 10 years," Gore said.
The panel he chaired also recommended that so-called enhanced ground proximity warning systems be installed in all commercial and military passenger aircraft.

Gore said this digital display would mean that "never again will an airplane like the one (late Commerce Secretary) Ron Brown was flying on ... not have a clear and timely warning to the pilot ... that a hill or mountain is ahead."
Brown died last April when the military plane in which he was flying crashed into a hillside in Croatia.
The White House Commission on Aviation, Safety and Security was formed at President Bill Clinton's request in response to last July's crash of TWA flight 800 near New York, which killed 230 people.

The commission, which included representatives of government as well as private citizens with relatives who died in recent air disasters, presented its recommendations to Clinton on Wednesday afternoon.

It said aviation security was a national security issue and the federal governent should provide "substantial funding" for capital improvements linked to safety. It recommended spending $100 million a year on capital requirements identified by the Federal Aviation Administration.
The panel recommended that the FAA draw up a plan within six months for developing by the year 2005 a satellite-based air traffic control system to update the current ground-based system.
To combat terror, the panel recommended that a "bag match" system linked to selecting, or "profiling" passengers be implemented no later than December of this year.
That would mean that a bag that had not been screened and that belonged to a passenger selected for extra scrutiny would not be allowed on board a plane, commissioners said.
The panel said the U.S. Postal Service should be given the authority to screen suspicious mail, and randomly screen all mail weighing over a pound for potential explosive devices.

The commission commended an airline industry initiative to equip cargo holds of passenger aircraft with smoke detectors, a matter that was an issue in the crash of a Valujet plane near Miami last May in which 110 lives were lost.

But commissioner Victoria Cummock said she dissented from this provision because it did not go far enough, and set no timetable. She added that the provision "does nothing to protect the flying public" from smoke and fumes in the cabin.
